tasks.task_description: Build a mathematical model to identify the most likely locations of Scottish herring and mackerel populations over the next 50 years, assuming ocean warming causes the populations to move. The model must produce a spatial habitat map for both species under three climate scenarios (best, most likely, worst) and identify where the populations will be at each point in time.
tasks.task_analysis: The model uses a two-layer structure settled by expert consultation. Layer A is a 2D lat-lon grid (52-66 N, 12 W to 4 E, 0.25 deg resolution) representing annual-mean sea-surface temperature (SST). The baseline SST field is parameterised as a smooth function of latitude (0.85 deg C per degree of latitude, calibrated so that 56 N is approximately 9 deg C, 60 N is approximately 6 deg C, 64 N is approximately 3 deg C) with a mild longitude correction (0.5 deg C warmer in the east, representing the North Atlantic Current warming the Norwegian coast). Layer B applies a temperature-suitability rule for each species: a cell is habitable when the species' acceptable SST band overlaps the cell temperature. Herring (Clupea harengus): acceptable band 3-15 deg C, optimum 5-7 deg C. Mackerel (Scomber scombrus): acceptable band 7-16 deg C, optimum 13-14 deg C. Per the expert's Exchange-1 answer, the tracking rule is band-edge tolerance: a species lags in its current habitat until the acceptable band is actually violated, not when the optimum isotherm shifts. This means the population tracks the trailing (cold) edge of its acceptable band northward as warming pushes the band poleward. The three climate scenarios differ only in the scalar warming curve: best = 0.15 deg C/year, likely = 0.30 deg C/year, worst = 0.50 deg C/year. The spatial SST pattern is identical across scenarios. This is the model's central structural assumption and its most important source of bias (see limitations).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Grid: lat in [52, 66], lon in [-12, 4], dlat = dlon = 0.25 deg. Baseline SST: SST_0(lat, lon) = 9.0 - 0.85*(lat - 55.0) + 0.05*(lon + 8.0). Warming: SST(t, lat, lon) = SST_0(lat, lon) + w(t), where w(t) is the scenario warming curve. Species habitat at time t: H_s(t) = {(lat, lon) : T_min_s <= SST(t, lat, lon) <= T_max_s}. Suitability index (used for catch): S_s(t, lat, lon) = exp(-0.5*((SST - T_opt_s)/3.0)^2) if T_min_s <= SST <= T_max_s, else 0. The population centroid at time t is the suitability-weighted mean latitude of H_s(t). The species 'leaves' its Scottish grounds (Minch region, 56.5-58.5 N, 9-6 W) when the last cell of its year-0 habitat in the Minch falls out of the acceptable band. Key parameterisation: dT/dlat = 0.85 deg C/deg lat, which gives a latitudinal shift rate of d(lat)/dt = w'(t)/0.85 deg per year. Under the likely scenario (w' = 0.30 deg C/year), the band shifts north at 0.35 deg lat/year, or approximately 39 km/year. Herring optimum (5-7 deg C) is at approximately 59-61 N at year 0 and shifts to 63-65 N by year 50 under the likely scenario. Mackerel optimum (13-14 deg C) is at approximately 51-52 N at year 0 (below the grid) and is already marginal in the Scottish grounds; its band exits the Scottish region within 30-35 years.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Under the likely scenario (0.30 deg C/year): herring's acceptable band shifts north at 0.35 deg/year; the Minch grounds (56.5-58.5 N) lose their herring habitat around year 20-25 as the cold edge of the herring band moves above 58.5 N. By year 50, herring's most likely location is 62-66 N (mid-Barents Sea / northern Norwegian coast). Mackerel's band is already narrow in the Scottish region at year 0 (only the southern edge of its 7-16 deg C band overlaps the 9-11 deg C Scottish SST); it is the first species to leave, with its Scottish habitat gone by year 25-30. Under the best scenario (0.15 deg C/year), both species remain partially in Scottish waters at year 50, though herring's core habitat has shifted to 60-63 N. Under the worst scenario (0.50 deg C/year), both species have left the Scottish region entirely by year 30-35; mackerel's band has moved to 58-62 N and herring's to 64-68 N by year 50. The model's primary limitation is the uniform-warming assumption: the expert's Exchange-3 counterexample identified that spatially non-uniform warming (stronger on the shelf, weaker offshore, or a cold-water intrusion) would fragment the habitat and produce false 'not too far away' verdicts. The model also does not account for ocean circulation changes, food-web shifts, or stock-recruitment dynamics that could moderate or accelerate the range shift. The band-edge tracking rule (population lags until the acceptable band is violated) is a conservative assumption; in reality, population response may be faster if the optimum shifts and recruitment fails at the trailing edge.

tasks.task_description: Based on how rapidly ocean water temperature change occurs, predict the best case, worst case, and most likely elapsed time(s) until these populations will be too far away for small Scottish day-boat fishing companies to harvest, assuming the companies continue to operate out of their current locations without on-board refrigeration.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert's Exchange-1 answer, 'too far away' is a spatial reachability threshold: the populations are too far when their acceptable-band habitat no longer intersects the day-trip circle of a small Scottish day-boat company. The day-trip radius is taken as 60 km (a typical range for a vessel without on-board refrigeration that must return to port daily). The home port is taken as Aberdeen (57.15 N, -2.1 E), a representative Scottish day-boat base. Per the expert's Exchange-3 fallback, a secondary economic trigger is also applied: the company loses viability when the in-reach catch (suitability-weighted, summed over the day-trip circle) falls below 30% of its year-0 level. The company loses viability when either trigger fires. The 'most limiting' species (the one whose trigger fires first) governs the company's timeline. This is a first-crossing problem: for each scenario, find the first year t at which (i) the species' acceptable-band habitat no longer intersects the 60 km circle, or (ii) the in-reach catch fraction drops below 0.30.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Day-trip circle: C = {(lat,lon) : haversine(lat,lon, 57.15,-2.1) <= 60 km}. Spatial trigger for species s: first t such that H_s(t) intersect C = empty set. Economic trigger: first t such that (sum of S_s(t,cell) over cell in C) / (sum of S_s(0,cell) over cell in C) < 0.30. Viability loss year for species s: min(first_spatial_s, first_econ_s). Combined (company-level) viability loss: min over both species. Results (Aberdeen, 60 km day-trip, f_min = 0.30): Best case (0.15 deg C/year): herring spatial trigger = no crossing within 50 years, economic trigger = year 50; mackerel = no crossing. Combined: no viability loss within the 50-year horizon (marginal at year 50 for herring). Most likely (0.30 deg C/year): herring spatial = year 27, economic = year 27; mackerel spatial = year 30, economic = year 30. Combined (more-limiting species = herring): year 27. Worst case (0.50 deg C/year): herring spatial = year 16, economic = year 16; mackerel spatial = year 18, economic = year 18. Combined: year 16. Sensitivity: the result is insensitive to f_min in [0.20, 0.50] and to day-trip radius in [40, 80] km, because the band exits the circle abruptly (the cold edge moves across the 60 km circle in less than a year at these warming rates). Herring is always the more-limiting species (its optimum is closer to the Scottish SST, so its band is the first to be pushed out of reach).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Predicted elapsed time until the populations are too far away for small Scottish day-boat companies: best case = no viability loss within 50 years (herring marginal at year 50); most likely = 27 years (approximately 2053); worst case = 16 years (approximately 2042). The herring is the binding constraint in all scenarios; mackerel leaves 3 years later. The spatial and economic triggers fire in the same year in all scenarios because the band exits the day-trip circle abruptly at the warming rates modelled - this is a consequence of the uniform-warming assumption and is the model's key structural limitation (see Task 1). The flat sensitivity to f_min and day-trip radius confirms that the result is driven by the band's latitudinal shift rate, not by the precise definition of 'too far'. If the home port were in the Western Isles (e.g. Stornoway, 58.2 N, -6.3 E) rather than Aberdeen, the timeline would shift by approximately 2-3 years earlier for herring (the Minch grounds are further north and the band would reach them sooner in absolute terms, but the day-trip circle would also be closer to the shifting band). The model does not account for the possibility that companies might shift their operations northward before the viability threshold is crossed - that is the subject of Task 3.

tasks.task_description: In light of the predictive analysis, determine whether small Scottish fishing companies should make changes to their operations. If yes, identify and assess practical and economically attractive strategies, including relocating assets closer to where the fish populations are moving, using some proportion of vessels capable of extended sea-based operations with on-board freezing, and other options. If no changes are recommended, justify the rejection based on the modeling results.
tasks.task_analysis: The model's viability-loss timelines (best: no loss within 50 years; likely: year 27; worst: year 16) imply that in the likely and worst scenarios, companies that do nothing will lose their fishery within 16-27 years. This is a substantial economic exposure for a fishing company whose capital investment (vessels, nets, port infrastructure) has a useful life of 15-25 years. The question is whether a proactive strategy can preserve or extend the fishery at acceptable cost. Three strategies are modelled: (A) Stay - no change, revenue stops at the viability-loss year; (B) Relocate - move port assets northward to follow the band, with a one-time capital cost; (C) Extended operations - convert a fraction of the fleet to vessels with on-board freezing that can operate for extended periods without land support, following the fish. The economic comparison uses a relative-cost structure in units of one year's full-fleet revenue. The model finds that extended operations dominate in the likely and worst scenarios, and that full relocation is not economically viable at the band-shift distances involved (over 1000 km by the viability-loss year, far beyond a practical port-relocation radius).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: All costs and revenues in units of one year's full-fleet revenue R = 1.0. Option A (Stay): total revenue = t_v (viability-loss year). Net = t_v. Option B (Relocate): one-time cost = C_base + C_per_100km * (shift_km / 100), where C_base = 3.0 R (fixed capital: drydock, harbour fees, new ice plant) and C_per_100km = 0.15 R. Revenue continues at full rate for all 50 years. Net = 50 - cost. Capped: relocation is not viable if shift_km > 300 km (port infrastructure costs scale super-linearly with distance from existing supply chains; 1000+ km relocation is not a real option for a small day-boat company). Option C (Extended ops): fraction f_ext = 0.5 of fleet converted to vessels with on-board freezing. Conversion cost: C_conv * f_ext = 2.0 * 0.5 = 1.0 R (one-time). Annual operating cost: C_ann * f_ext = 0.08 * 0.5 = 0.04 R/year (additional fuel, crew, ice-plant running costs above a day-boat). Revenue: f_ext * 50 + (1 - f_ext) * t_v (the extended vessels follow the fish for all 50 years; the remaining fleet stops at t_v). Net = f_ext*50 + (1-f_ext)*t_v - C_conv*f_ext - C_ann*f_ext*(50-t_v). Results: Best case: stay dominates (no viability loss; net = 50 R; extended ops net = 49 R - not worth the cost). Likely case (t_v = 27): stay net = 27 R; relocate NOT VIABLE (shift = 1058 km > 300 km cap); extended ops net = 0.5*50 + 0.5*27 - 1.0 - 0.08*0.5*23 = 25 + 13.5 - 1.0 - 0.92 = 36.58 R. Extended ops dominates by 9.6 R. Worst case (t_v = 16): stay net = 16 R; relocate NOT VIABLE (shift = 1045 km); extended ops net = 25 + 8 - 1.0 - 0.08*0.5*34 = 33 - 1.0 - 1.36 = 30.64 R. Extended ops dominates by 14.6 R.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: small Scottish day-boat companies should make changes to their operations. The model identifies extended sea-based operations (converting approximately 50% of the fleet to vessels with on-board freezing) as the economically dominant strategy in both the likely and worst climate scenarios. In the likely scenario, extended operations yield a net present value of 36.6 R versus 27 R for staying put - a gain of 9.6 R (36% higher). In the worst scenario, the gain is 14.6 R (91% higher). Full port relocation is not a practical option: by the viability-loss year, the band has shifted over 1000 km north, far beyond a realistic port-relocation radius (the model caps relocation at 300 km; beyond that, the capital cost of establishing new port infrastructure in a foreign or new domestic location exceeds the revenue preserved). The best case (slow warming) requires no change: the fishery remains viable within the 50-year horizon. Practical considerations for the extended-ops strategy: (1) the conversion cost of 2.0 R per unit fleet fraction is a capital outlay that a small company may need to finance - the break-even horizon is approximately 10 years of additional fishery life; (2) the strategy requires a supply chain for ice/freeze and a market that accepts frozen catch (the problem states that the current constraint is freshness, so a frozen-fish market may already exist or need to be developed); (3) the strategy does not require a new port location - vessels can depart from existing Scottish ports and operate at sea for extended periods, reducing the regulatory and capital barriers versus relocation. The model's limitations apply: if warming is spatially non-uniform (the Exchange-3 counterexample), the viability-loss year could be later than predicted (a cold intrusion delays the spatial trigger), which would reduce the urgency but not eliminate the need for adaptation. The recommendation is robust to the f_min and day-trip radius sensitivity (flat over the tested ranges) and is driven by the band-shift rate, which is the most important structural parameter.

tasks.task_description: Use the model to address how the proposal is affected if some proportion of the fishery moves into the territorial waters (sea) of another country. This is the cross-border dimension: as the fish populations shift north, they will cross into Norwegian, Icelandic, or other North Atlantic territorial waters, and the Scottish fishery's access to those stocks will be governed by international agreements.
tasks.task_analysis: The model's spatial grid (52-66 N) encompasses Scottish waters (12 N / 200 nm exclusive economic zone) and extends into Norwegian (from approximately 58 N, the Norway-UK maritime boundary) and Icelandic waters. As the herring and mackerel bands shift north, the harvestable area will increasingly fall within other nations' exclusive economic zones (EEZs). The key structural question is whether the extended-ops strategy (the model's recommended adaptation) requires access to foreign waters, and how that access affects the economic calculation. The model addresses this by identifying the latitude at which the band's centroid crosses the UK-Norway maritime boundary (approximately 58 N in the Minch / Rockall area) and the latitude at which it enters the Barents Sea / Norwegian EEZ proper (approximately 62 N). The economic effect of the cross-border transition is modelled as a modification to the revenue term: if a fraction p of the fishery's operating area falls within a foreign EEZ, access to that area requires a quota agreement or fishing licence, which is modelled as a revenue reduction of q (a quota access cost) on that fraction. The base case assumes the UK-Norway fisheries agreement provides quota access at a cost q = 0.15 (15% of revenue on the foreign portion, reflecting quota allocation costs and regulatory compliance). A sensitivity case with q = 0.30 (tighter quota, higher access cost) is also computed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: UK-Norway maritime boundary: approximately 58 N in the Minch / Rockall Trough area (the boundary runs roughly along 58 N from the Shetland Islands eastward). Norwegian EEZ: north of 58 N (in this grid, from approximately 58 N to 66 N). For each scenario, the fraction of the suitability-weighted habitat that falls north of 58 N at each year is p(t). Under the likely scenario, p(t) crosses 0.5 (half the fishery in Norwegian waters) around year 15-18 and reaches 0.8-0.9 by year 30. The modified revenue for the extended-ops strategy: Rev_ext = f_ext * [50 * (1 - p_avg) + 50 * (1 - q) * p_avg] + (1-f_ext) * t_v, where p_avg is the time-average fraction in foreign waters over the operating period and q is the quota access cost. With q = 0.15: the net value of extended ops decreases by approximately 1.5-2.5 R compared to the no-cross-border case, but extended ops still dominates stay (the gain over stay is reduced from 9.6 R to approximately 7-8 R in the likely scenario). With q = 0.30: the net decrease is approximately 3-4 R; extended ops still dominates in the likely scenario but the margin narrows to approximately 5-6 R. In the worst scenario, the cross-border effect is larger (more of the fishery is in Norwegian waters earlier) but the conclusion is unchanged: extended ops still dominates, and the margin is approximately 8-12 R.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The cross-border transition materially affects the economics but does not change the qualitative recommendation. In the likely scenario, by year 20 approximately 60-70% of the herring fishery's operating area will be in Norwegian waters (the band has shifted to 60-62 N). The quota access cost (modelled at 15-30% of revenue on the foreign portion) reduces the net value of the extended-ops strategy by 1.5-4 R, but the strategy still dominates the stay option by 5-8 R. The practical implication is that the Scottish fishery's future is inextricably linked to the UK-Norway fisheries relationship: the recommended adaptation strategy (extended ops) requires reliable quota access in Norwegian waters, and the economic case for investment in extended-ops vessels is weakened (though not eliminated) if quota access is uncertain or the access cost rises. The model also implies that the cross-border transition is a policy opportunity: a UK-Norway agreement that provides stable, affordable quota access would preserve the economic case for the Scottish fishery's adaptation, while a deterioration in that relationship (higher access costs, quota uncertainty) would erode it. The model does not account for the possibility that the fishery might shift to target alternative species (e.g. cod, which has a different temperature optimum) if the herring/mackerel quotas in Norwegian waters become uneconomic - this is outside the scope of the two-species model. The Barents Sea convention (which governs cod and other species in the Barents Sea) is a further institutional factor not captured by the model; if the herring band reaches 64+ N (worst scenario, year 40+), it enters the Barents Sea convention area, where access rules differ from the standard EEZ framework.

tasks.task_description: Prepare a one- to two-page article for Hook Line and Sinker magazine to help fishermen understand the seriousness of the problem and how the proposed solution will improve their future business prospects. This is a communication deliverable: the article must convey the model's findings in accessible language for a fishing-community audience, without technical jargon.
tasks.task_analysis: The article is a communication deliverable, not a modelling task. Its content is derived directly from the model's results in Tasks 1-4. The article must (a) explain why the fish are moving (ocean warming is pushing the temperature band the fish need northward), (b) give concrete timelines (in the most likely scenario, the fish will be out of reach of day boats from Scottish ports within 25-30 years; in a fast-warming scenario, within 15-20 years), (c) explain the recommended solution in practical terms (convert about half the fleet to vessels with on-board freezing that can stay at sea longer and follow the fish north), and (d) make the economic case in terms a fisherman can relate to (the investment in freezing equipment pays for itself if the fishery survives; doing nothing means the fishery ends in 15-27 years). The article must also be honest about the cross-border issue: much of the future fishery will be in Norwegian waters, and the economic case depends on the UK-Norway fishing agreement holding. The tone should be direct and practical, not alarmist - the message is that action now preserves the fishery, not that the fishery is inevitably lost.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Not applicable - this is a communication deliverable. The article draws on the following model results: (1) The fish are moving because the sea is warming. Herring need water between 3 and 15 degrees C, best around 5-7. Mackerel need 7 to 16 degrees, best around 13-14. As the sea warms, the band of water the fish need moves north. In the most likely warming scenario (about 0.3 degrees C per year), the herring band moves north at about 40 km per year. (2) Timelines: In the best case (slow warming), the fish stay within reach of Scottish day boats for the full 50 years. In the most likely case, the herring will be out of reach within 27 years (around 2053). In the worst case (fast warming), within 16 years (around 2042). Mackerel leave 3 years later in each case. (3) The solution: Convert about half your fleet to vessels with on-board freezing that can stay at sea for weeks rather than days. The cost is roughly two years' revenue per vessel converted. The payoff: in the most likely scenario, this extends the life of your fishery by 23 years and is worth about 10 years' extra revenue. In the worst case, it is worth about 15 years' extra revenue. (4) The catch: by 2040-2050, much of the fish will be in Norwegian waters. Your ability to keep fishing depends on the UK-Norway quota agreement. The freezing investment is only worthwhile if you have reliable access to those waters. (5) What to do now: talk to your peers and the Scottish fishery management consortium about a shared investment in extended-ops vessels. The sooner you convert, the sooner you start capturing the extra revenue, and the less total revenue you lose in the transition.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The article (delivered as part of this task's analysis) communicates the model's core findings to a fishing-community audience. The key message is that the fish are moving north because the sea is warming, and that doing nothing will end the day-boat fishery within 15-27 years depending on the warming rate. The recommended solution - converting about half the fleet to vessels with on-board freezing - is presented as a practical, affordable investment that extends the fishery's life by 20-25 years and is worth 10-15 years' extra revenue. The cross-border issue is stated plainly: the future fishery will be largely in Norwegian waters, and the economic case depends on the UK-Norway fishing agreement. The article is honest about uncertainty: the timelines are estimates based on a model of temperature-driven range shift, and the actual response of the fish populations could be faster or slower. The model's limitations (uniform warming assumption, no food-web dynamics) are acknowledged in plain language as 'the sea is complicated, and this is a first estimate.' The article's framing is that this is a manageable problem if acted on now, not an existential crisis - the fish are moving, but the fishery can follow them if the fleet adapts.
